data_description.discharged_energy_entity: The counterpart: total energy taken out, in kWh.

data_description.health_entity: State of health in percent, if the BMS reports it.

data_description.min_soc: Discharge stops here. Remaining runtime is calculated against this limit.
data_description.model: Display only, e.g. the type designation from the label.
data_description.name: Name of this storage, e.g. “Battery 48 V cellar”.
data_description.nominal_voltage: Voltage level of the storage - 24 V or 48 V are common. Display only.
data_description.power_entity: Charge and discharge power. If absent, voltage × current is used.
data_description.power_sign: This is the direct battery power. You decide which sign means charging: “+ = charging” is the usual case, some BMS count the other way round. Chosen wrongly the card swaps charging and discharging.
data_description.soc_entity: State of charge in percent, usually from the BMS. Without it stored energy and runtime stay empty.
data_description.voltage_entity: Terminal voltage of the battery (e.g. 51.8 V on a 48 V system).

data_description.input_voltage_entity: The voltage coming from the modules - often three digits on an MPPT.
data_description.manufacturer: Display only - the card shows manufacturer and model together.
data_description.max_current: Display only, e.g. 85 A on a 250/85 MPPT.
data_description.model: Display only, e.g. the type designation from the label.
data_description.name: Name of this controller, e.g. “MPPT roof east”.
data_description.output_current_entity: Charging current towards the battery. Without a power sensor the charging power is computed from it.
data_description.output_voltage_entity: The voltage on the battery side, i.e. 24 V, 48 V and so on.
data_description.power_entity: Charging power towards the battery. If absent it is computed from output voltage × output current.
data_description.system_voltage: Voltage level of the battery behind it - 24 V or 48 V are common. Shown as a badge on the card.
data_description.temperature_entity: Temperature of the controller itself, not of the battery.
data_description.yield_entity: kWh meter that many MPPT controllers provide.

data.base_price_entity: Base fee: entity instead of fixed number
data.feed_in_entity: Feed-in tariff: entity instead of fixed number
data.price_entity: Energy price: entity instead of fixed number

data_description.base_price:
The base fee of your electricity contract - meter and network charges, everything that is due regardless of consumption. **Whether the number is for a month or a year is set in the field below.**

It is spread proportionally across day, month and year. Empty or 0 if you do not want it counted here.
data_description.base_price_entity: The same for the base fee. Note: what this entity provides is read with the period above - if that says “per year”, it applies to the entity too.
data_description.base_price_unit: Which period the number above refers to. Many contracts state the base fee per year, many bills per month - both are fine, it just has to be said here. Internally the monthly figure is used; “per year” is divided by twelve.
data_description.currency: The currency code, e.g. EUR or CHF. It is used as the unit of the money sensors.
data_description.feed_in_entity: The same for the feed-in tariff.
data_description.feed_in_price: What you are paid per kilowatt hour fed into the grid, e.g. 0.08. Leave empty if you do not export.
data_description.price_entity: An entity providing the energy price - for dynamic tariffs. It takes precedence over the fixed number above; if it reports nothing usable, the number applies again. Empty: the fixed number only.
data_description.price_per_kwh: What one kilowatt hour from the grid costs, e.g. 0.34. Without this price no costs are calculated and no money sensors are created.
data_description.prior_import:
**Your import meter's reading on the day you set this integration up.** A one-off number you read once and never touch again - not a sensor.

Example: your import meter reads 5000 kWh today and you set up today. Then you enter 5000.

What for: from today the integration only counts differences. Without this number the total period would start at zero grid cost and the balance would look better than it is. Day, month and year are untouched.

Empty: the total period starts today. That is right if you only want to count from now on.
data_description.prior_price: What one kilowatt hour cost on average before the integration started counting - electricity three years ago was not priced like today. Applies to that earlier time only. Empty: today's price is used.

costs.description:
Everything is derived from the meter readings you entered under “Grid and meter” - not from extrapolated power. Day, month and year start counting the moment you enter a price here - the time before is covered by the figures at each plant.

You may change the price at any time: only what has accrued since the last calculation is valued. A price increase applies from the day you enter it and does not rewrite the past.

What a plant cost and since when it runs belongs to that plant under “Costs of this plant”. The site's investment is the sum of its plants, its start the earliest commissioning - nobody needs to enter either again here.

**Wherever an entity and a fixed number sit side by side, the entity always wins.** The number is only the fallback for when the entity reports nothing usable - a stalled tariff fetch, a sensor gone unavailable.

Almost everything may be left empty. What you leave out simply is not shown on the card - only the fields marked with * are required.
costs.title: Costs and yield

data_description.animate: The dots on the lines move with the power. Off if the dashboard stutters on an old tablet.
data_description.sensor_interval: How often this integration's measurement sensors may write a new value to the database. The card does not depend on it - it reads along directly and stays second by second. 0 means: on every measurement, and that makes the database grow fast.
data_description.show_phases: Three phase lines between meter and house, each with its own flow. Off leaves a single AC line - right for a single-phase system and noticeably flatter.
data_description.show_strings: Draws the modules individually, in series and parallel. Off gives a narrower card.

data_description.export_energy_entity:
The counterpart: a kWh counter that only rises and counts what went to the grid.

The feed-in revenue comes from it. With several plants it is split by each plant's share of generation - it cannot be measured, there is one meter for all of them at the house connection.

Empty: no revenue. If you never export, leave it empty.
data_description.export_power_entity: Counterpart to import power - likewise only needed with separate meters.
data_description.frequency_entity: One field is enough: in a synchronous grid all three phases share the same frequency - they are rigidly locked together. One value per phase would be the same number three times.
data_description.import_energy_entity:
**The single most important meter here.** A kWh counter that only rises and counts what you drew from the grid - in Home Assistant usually a Riemann sum over your meter's import power.

All money comes from it: grid costs for day, month, year and total. The integration remembers its reading on the first run and only counts differences from then on - so the meter may have been running for years, today's reading costs nothing.

Empty: no grid costs, no balance, no payback.
data_description.import_power_entity: Only needed if your meter reports import and export separately instead of one signed figure.
data_description.l1_current_entity: Current on L1, in A. Purely informative.
data_description.l1_power_entity: Power on L1. Leave empty if you only have the total meter - the card then does not draw phases individually.
data_description.l1_voltage_entity: Voltage on L1, around 230 V. Purely informative.
data_description.l2_current_entity: Current on L2, in A. Purely informative.
data_description.l2_power_entity: Power on L2 - like L1 only needed if your meter reports phases individually.
data_description.l2_voltage_entity: Voltage on L2, around 230 V. Purely informative.
data_description.l3_current_entity: Current on L3, in A. Purely informative.
data_description.l3_power_entity: Power on L3 - like L1 only needed if your meter reports phases individually.
data_description.l3_voltage_entity: Voltage on L3, around 230 V. Purely informative.
data_description.name: Name of the grid connection. It sits above the box on the card.
data_description.phases: Phases of the house connection. Almost always three - only change it if you know otherwise.
data_description.power_entity: The total across all phases at the house connection. The most important field here.
data_description.power_sign: How the meter counts. Chosen wrongly the card shows the flow reversed.

grid.description:
The total meter is enough. If phases are measured individually the card draws them separately.

Almost everything may be left empty. What you leave out simply is not shown on the card - only the fields marked with * are required.
grid.title: Grid and meter

data_description.calculate: Consumption = inverter power + grid power. A measured value takes precedence.
data_description.energy_entity:
A kWh counter over **everything consumed in the house** - grid import *and* self-used solar together. Not the import meter: that one lives under “Grid and meter” and only counts what came from the grid.

What for: it is the second route to self-consumption. Normally the integration computes “generated minus exported”; without a yield meter it falls back to “consumed minus imported” - and that is what this is for.

Empty: perfectly fine as long as your plants have a yield meter.
data_description.power_entity:
Only if you **measure** house consumption - with a second meter behind the house connection, say. In watts, not a meter reading.

Normally leave it empty: the integration then derives it from grid power plus inverter output, which for a grid-parallel system is just as correct.

data_description.mode_entity: Operating mode as text, e.g. “grid-tied” or “off-grid”.
data_description.model: Display only, e.g. the type designation from the label.

data_description.power_entity: AC output power - the built-in sensor or an inline meter such as a inline meter. House consumption is derived from this figure.
data_description.rated_power_w: Continuous rating from the label. The load bar is based on it.

Designed for single-phase inverters running in parallel with the grid.

data_description.energy_entity: A kWh meter for this array's yield, if you have one. May be left empty.
data_description.model: The module type, e.g. “Vertex S 405”. Display only.
data_description.parallel: Four in series, two such strings in parallel makes eight modules.
data_description.peak_wp: Peak power of a single module as printed on its label.

data_description.commissioned: Since when this plant has been running. Without this date the payback starts on the day you set up the integration - and the remaining time would be years off.
data_description.feed_in_price: Only fill this in if this plant gets a different tariff from the rest. Two plants from two years regularly have two rates. Empty: the rate under “Costs and yield” applies.
data_description.investment: What this plant cost - modules, charge controller, storage, inverter, mounting. Its payback is derived from it.
data_description.prior_export:
**How much of “yield meter reading” went to the grid** - also as of the setup day, also one-off.

What for: the remainder (yield minus export) counts as self-used and is valued at the energy price; the exported part at **this** plant's tariff. Two plants from two years regularly have two rates - which is why this lives here and not at the site.

Empty or 0: everything before counts as self-used. If you never exported, that is correct.
data_description.prior_yield:
**This plant's yield meter reading on the day you set the integration up.** Usually shown on the inverter. A one-off number, not a sensor.

Example: the plant has run since 2024 and produced 2300 kWh, you set up today - so 2300.

What for: these kilowatt hours count towards this plant's yield and thus towards **its payback**. Without them a 2024 plant would look as if it had only just started. Total period only; day, month and year are untouched.

plant_costs.description:
What this plant cost and since when it has been running. Both count for this plant alone: with several plants each gets its own payback, and the site's is their sum.

Almost everything may be left empty. What you leave out simply is not shown on the card - only the fields marked with * are required.
plant_costs.title: Costs – {plant}

data.reset_confirm: Yes, discard the measured cost figures
data.reset_prior: Yes, also remove the “before” figures from the configuration

reset.description:
The way out when the amounts no longer add up - typically after a meter swap, or when the wrong entity briefly sat in the import meter field. Day, month and year heal themselves at the next rollover; the total period carries the error until somebody clears it.

The total period has **two sources**, which is why there are two checkboxes.

---

**1. Measured since the first run**

{stand}

This lives in the integration's own store. The first box throws it away and re-anchors every counter at today's reading - immediately, not on save.

---

**2. From the configuration: the “before” figures**

{vorher}

That is where amounts come from that stand next to zero measured kilowatt hours and are still correct. The second box removes those fields from the configuration - it only takes effect with “Save and close”.

Usually you do **not** want it: these numbers are your real history, and without them the payback starts at zero. It helps if you mistyped or want to start over.

Investment and commissioning stay either way - those are facts about the system, not meter readings. Neither can be undone.
reset.title: Clear cost counters

data.diverter_price: Price of what is replaced: fixed number
data.diverter_price_entity: Price of what is replaced: entity instead of fixed number
data.diverter_price_unit: Price of what is replaced: per

data_description.diverter_efficiency:
How much heat the **replaced** heating makes from its fuel, in percent. It needs more than one kilowatt hour of fuel for one kilowatt hour of heat - that is the whole point.

• Condensing gas boiler: about **92**
• Older gas or oil boiler: **80** to **88**
• Pellet boiler: about **90**
• District heating: **100** - what arrives is heat, not fuel
• **Heat pump: the seasonal performance factor times a hundred.** At SPF 3.5 that is 350. It turns one kilowatt hour of electricity into three and a half kilowatt hours of heat - an immersion heater only into one. That is why surplus is worth much less in a house with a heat pump, and the calculation should say so.

100 means: do not convert.
data_description.diverter_energy_entity:
kWh counters of these loads. **Several are allowed** - they are added up.

These kilowatt hours really do flow in the house. Whether they save money depends on what they replace: heating with them instead of gas saves gas, not electricity - so they are valued separately in the savings, with the two fields further down.

Empty: the surplus counts like any other self-consumption.
data_description.diverter_fuel:
What this load replaces. It decides what one diverted kilowatt hour is worth.

Natural gas, LPG, oil, pellets, district heating or heat pump: the value is that fuel's price per kWh - see the fields below.

“Nothing - it stays electricity”: a home battery or a car burns nothing, it moves electricity to later. Then a kilowatt hour is worth exactly the energy price, and the fields below are ignored.
data_description.diverter_name: What the load is called on the card, e.g. “immersion heater”.
data_description.diverter_power_entity:
What the surplus loads currently draw - the immersion heater in the hot water tank, the wallbox in surplus charging, the heat pump's buffer tank. **Several are allowed**; they are added up.

This means everything that only runs **because** there is surplus and puts energy into a store - hot water, a car battery, a buffer tank. A fridge does not count: it runs anyway.

This power is subtracted from house consumption to give the **base load** - what your household would have used without the surplus. Self-sufficiency and self-consumption still use the **whole** house consumption; the base load stands beside it because only it is comparable from month to month.
data_description.diverter_price:
The price **as it appears on your bill** - not converted. Converting is the integration's job: it knows how many kilowatt hours are in a litre, a cubic metre or a tonne, and it asks for the efficiency below.

Which unit you mean is set in the field next to it. Natural gas is usually billed per kWh or per m³, LPG per litre or kilogram, heating oil per litre, pellets per tonne, district heating per kWh.

Because this changes constantly, the field below is usually the better one: an entity providing the price.

Empty: the energy price applies, and the system looks better off than it is.
data_description.diverter_price_entity:
An entity providing this price - **the better way for anything that moves with the market.** Gas and oil do, just like electricity; a fixed number is wrong tomorrow.

It takes precedence over the fixed number above; if it reports nothing usable, the number applies again. It means the same price in the same unit - conversion happens here too.
data_description.diverter_price_unit:
What the price refers to - **exactly as it is billed**. The integration converts it into kilowatt hours:

• Natural gas: per kWh or per m³ (about 10 kWh per m³)
• LPG: per litre (6.57 kWh), per kg (12.87 kWh)
• Heating oil: per litre (10 kWh), per kg (11.9 kWh)
• Pellets: per kg (4.8 kWh) or per tonne (4800 kWh)
• District heating and heat pump: per kWh

If the unit does not fit the fuel - there is no heating oil per cubic metre - nothing is converted and the energy price applies. Better no number than an invented one.

The calorific values are the usual ones; they vary by a few percent with quality. If you need it exact, enter the price per kilowatt hour directly.
data_description.diverter_solar_energy_entity:
The same as a kWh counter: the load's kilowatt hours that came from PV or battery. **Several are allowed.**

If set, only this counter feeds the savings - the remainder is ordinary grid consumption at the energy price.
data_description.diverter_solar_power_entity:
**Only if you can measure it separately.** The part of the power above that is currently coming from PV or battery.

Why it matters: an immersion heater runs on surplus in July and on grid power in January. The same kilowatt hour is free energy once and a full-price bill the next time. Only the part that came from your own system is valued with the price of what it replaces.

Empty: what the name says applies - all of it came from surplus. For a true surplus controller that is correct.

surplus.description:
Loads that **only run because there is surplus** and put energy into a store: the immersion heater in the hot water tank, the wallbox in surplus charging, the heat pump's buffer tank. A fridge does not count - it runs anyway.

They are a topic of their own because their kilowatt hours **replace not electricity but gas, oil, heat** - and are therefore valued differently from any other self-consumption.

Everything here may be left empty. If you have no such load, skip this step.

**Wherever an entity and a fixed number sit side by side, the entity always wins.** The number is only the fallback for when the entity reports nothing usable. The same applies to energy price, feed-in tariff and base fee.
surplus.title: Surplus

tidy.description:
This integration creates a sensor for every value. If the value comes from exactly the entity you configured yourself, it then exists twice in Home Assistant - and writes to the database twice.

Newly set up systems do not need this: there these sensors are off from the start. It is needed once only if you set up before version 1.1.1.

Only entities of this integration are affected. Nothing is deleted: each one stays in the device view and can be brought back with one click.

{liste}
